**Paper**: [Logical Reasoning with Outcome Reward Models for Test-Time Scaling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.19903v1)

## TL;DR

Paper trains Outcome Reward Models for deductive text-LLM reasoning + test-time scaling. Repo is inference-only VLM spatial-reasoning eval — no trainer, no reward-model path, no logic benchmark, no scoped call site. Decide fit.

## Suggested experiment

Scope a test-time-selection harness that fits the existing inference-only path: for each spatial-reasoning benchmark item, have the VLM generate N candidate answers, score each with a lightweight proxy reward (reuse `evaluation.py`'s ground-truth scoring as a stand-in for a learned ORM), and measure the accuracy lift from best-of-N selection over the single-shot baseline. This tests whether ORM-style test-time scaling transfers to the spatial VLM setting before investing in training a real reward model.

## Engineering analysis

The paper contributes three things, all centered on **text LLMs doing deductive logic**:

- A set of trained **Outcome Reward Models (ORMs)** that score whether an LLM's reasoning trace reaches a correct conclusion on deductive-reasoning tasks.
- A **training recipe** for those ORMs (needs a trainer, supervised/RL data, and a model head).
- A **test-time scaling recipe**: generate N candidate reasoning traces, score each with the ORM, select the best.

This is fundamentally an LLM logical-reasoning method: text in, text out, built on a reward-modeling + training pipeline.

### What blocks a clean implementation

- **Modality and domain mismatch.** vqasynth is an **inference + evaluation pipeline for visual spatial reasoning** over VLMs (`benchmarks.py`, `evaluation.py`, `inference.py`, plus `depth`/`localize`/`scene_fusion`). The paper targets **deductive logical reasoning** over text LLMs. There is no logical-reasoning benchmark, no text-only LLM path, and no spatial ↔ deductive bridge in the repo.
- **No training infrastructure.** The paper's core contribution is *training* ORMs and *selecting among candidates via reward scores*. vqasynth is inference-only — there is no trainer, no reward-model head, and no candidate-generate + score + select harness. `r1_reasoning.py` does reasoning prompting but not ORM-scored best-of-N selection.
- **No scoped call site identified.** No candidate-selection rationale named a subset or call site against this module layout, so there is no implementable slice that drops into existing code. The most realistic implementation would be a freestanding test-time-selection module that nothing in the repo currently calls.

### How to unblock this

- **Is branching into deductive/logical reasoning in scope at all?** Given the repo's spatial-reasoning focus, this may simply be a poor fit. If not in scope, close out.
- **If the intent is to adapt ORM-style test-time scaling to VLM spatial reasoning**, that is a research effort (build candidate generation + reward scoring for spatial QA), not a drop-in PR — it needs explicit scoping and a sponsor.
- **If we just want to consume the paper's released ORM**, confirm (a) the authors released checkpoints with a usable loader, and (b) we're willing to stand up a text-LLM eval rail, since the current path is VLM/spatial. Either way this needs a decision before implementation.

## Why the orchestrator opened an Issue instead of a PR

**Pre-flight routed to Issue before implementation.** The paper's contribution is training Outcome Reward Models (ORMs) for deductive text-LLM reasoning and using them for test-time scaling, but vqasynth is an inference-only VLM spatial-reasoning eval pipeline — it has no trainer, no reward-model path, and no deductive-logic benchmark. No selection rationale named any call sites against the module layout, and the modality/domain mismatch (text logical reasoning vs. visual spatial reasoning) means even a scoped slice has nowhere natural to land. This needs a fit/scope decision before any PR.

## Background

- Parent: #43

Gameplay now has peer-owned points, badges, game results, reward grants, and pet workspaces. `GameRuleset` can define deterministic drive rewards, but Flowcraft pet workflows do not yet have a controlled toolkit surface for granting gameplay rewards from LLM-driven activities such as daily check-ins, guided tasks, or conversation milestones.

This issue adds a server-side gameplay reward tool that can be exposed to Flowcraft workflows. It is not a peer RPC for arbitrary reward grants, and it is not token/accounting. It is a constrained gameplay toolkit path that records normal `RewardGrant`, `PointsTransaction`, badge exp, and pet state changes through the same gameplay runtime rules.

## Goal

Add a controlled gameplay reward tool for Flowcraft pet workflows.

The end state is:

- admins can enable and bound the reward tool in `GameRuleset`;
- Flowcraft pet workflows can call one gameplay toolkit tool to grant configured gameplay rewards;
- all grants use the existing gameplay SQL resources as source of truth;
- grants are auditable through existing reward grant, points transaction, badge, and pet APIs;
- direct peer clients still cannot grant arbitrary rewards through RPC.

This issue owns the toolkit reward-grant path only. It does not own scheduled tasks, long-running quest tracking, token/accounting balances, or a public peer reward-grant RPC.

## Code Changes Tree

```text
api/
├── type/
│   └── gameplay.json                         # GameRuleset toolkit reward tool config
└── rpc/                                      # generated outputs if schema generation requires them

pkgs/gizclaw/
├── api/
│   ├── apitypes/                             # generated, committed
│   └── rpcapi/                               # generated, committed if affected
└── services/
    ├── gameplay/
    │   ├── reward_tool.go                    # toolkit grant validation and runtime entrypoint
    │   ├── reward.go                         # shared reward merge/apply helpers
    │   ├── runtime.go                        # calls into the reward tool implementation
    │   └── runtime_test.go                   # reward tool unit coverage
    ├── ai/workflow/agents/flowcraft/
    │   ├── factory.go                        # registers gameplay toolkit tools on Claw
    │   └── factory_test.go                   # Flowcraft tool registration/call coverage
    └── runtime/agenthost/
        ├── spec.go                           # passes gameplay toolkit dependencies to workflow agents if needed
        └── agenthost_test.go                 # host/factory wiring coverage

tests/
└── gizclaw-e2e/
    ├── go/gameplay/
    │   └── gameplay_toolkit_test.go          # workflow-triggered reward grant e2e
    └── testdata/resources/07-gameplay/
        └── 00-starter-gameplay.yaml          # ruleset enables bounded toolkit reward
```

## Design

### GameRuleset Configuration

Extend `GameRuleset.spec` with a toolkit section for reward tools:

```yaml
toolkit:
  reward_tools:
    gameplay_reward_grant:
      enabled: true
      max_points_delta: 20
      max_pet_exp_delta: 50
      allowed_badge_def_ids:
      - badge-starter
      allowed_life_stats:
      - hunger
      - thirst
      - clean
      allowed_ability_stats: []
      require_idempotency_key: true
```

The runtime must reject tool grants when:

- the ruleset is disabled;
- the reward tool is disabled;
- the pet does not belong to the caller/workspace owner;
- the requested deltas exceed configured bounds;
- badge, life, or ability keys are not allowed by the ruleset;
- `require_idempotency_key` is true and the request does not provide one;
- the idempotency key was already applied for the same owner and ruleset with a different payload.

### Tool Contract

Register one Flowcraft Claw tool for gameplay pet workflows:

```text
gameplay.reward_grant
```

Tool input:

```json
{
  "pet_id": "pet-...",
  "reason": "daily_chat_checkin",
  "idempotency_key": "workspace-event-id",
  "points_delta": 5,
  "pet_exp_delta": 10,
  "badge_exp_delta": {
    "badge-starter": 20
  },
  "life_delta": {
    "hunger": 5
  },
  "ability_delta": {}
}
```

Tool output:

```json
{
  "reward_grant_id": "grant-...",
  "points_balance": 105,
  "pet_exp": 120,
  "pet_level": 2,
  "badges": [
    {
      "id": "badge-...",
      "badge_def_id": "badge-starter",
      "exp": 120,
      "level": 1,
      "active": true
    }
  ]
}
```

The output is for the workflow to continue reasoning. The durable API surface remains the existing gameplay resources.

### Runtime Behavior

The reward tool must use the same gameplay mutation path as drive rewards:

1. Resolve the pet and ruleset.
2. Validate the tool request against `GameRuleset.spec.toolkit.reward_tools`.
3. Start one SQL transaction.
4. Ensure the points account exists.
5. Insert one `RewardGrant` with `source_type = "llm_reward_tool"` and `source_id = idempotency_key`.
6. Apply pet life, ability, exp, and level deltas.
7. Apply badge exp and badge level updates.
8. Insert points transactions for non-zero point deltas.
9. Commit the transaction.
10. Return the committed identifiers and updated summary state.

The reward tool must not bypass `RewardGrant` or write directly to account/badge/pet rows.

### Flowcraft Integration

The Flowcraft agent factory should register the tool on the `flowclaw.Claw` instance only when the workspace is a gameplay pet workspace and the resolved ruleset enables the tool. Non-gameplay Flowcraft workspaces must not see the gameplay reward tool.

The tool handler should call a gameplay service interface rather than importing SQL/runtime internals directly into the Flowcraft workflow package. The dependency boundary should allow tests to use a fake gameplay toolkit service.

### Error Handling

Validation failures return a tool error message to the workflow and must not commit partial gameplay state.

Idempotency conflicts should return the previously committed grant when the stored request is equivalent. If the same idempotency key is reused with a different reward payload, return a validation/conflict error and do not mutate state.

### Boundaries

This issue does not add:

- peer RPC methods for granting rewards;
- admin UI for editing the toolkit config;
- scheduled task engines;
- token/accounting integration;
- arbitrary LLM-selected rewards without `GameRuleset` bounds.

## Test And Acceptance Criteria

- `go test ./pkgs/gizclaw/services/gameplay` covers:
  - successful toolkit reward grant;
  - points, badge exp, pet exp, life, and ability mutations;
  - idempotency success and conflicting replay;
  - disabled tool rejection;
  - bounds and allow-list rejection;
  - transaction rollback on validation or write errors.
- `go test ./pkgs/gizclaw/services/ai/workflow/agents/flowcraft ./pkgs/gizclaw/services/runtime/agenthost` covers:

## Context

v0.71.26 shipped **closed-loop reward-hacking auto-mitigation** — the GRPO/PPO trainer detects reward hacking mid-run and self-corrects (raise KL β via bang-bang or PID-Lagrangian → roll back to last-good checkpoint → early-stop), plus Stage-3 anti-gaming hardening (smoothing, conservative-on-disagreement voting, reward-distribution-drift guard, bounded reward shaping).

The mechanism is **validated as proof-of-mechanism only**: SmolLM2-135M + a *synthetic* length-hacking reward on a single RTX 3050. All four stages pass live, including a real mid-run rollback. See [`docs/training.md`](https://github.com/MakazhanAlpamys/Soup/blob/main/docs/training.md#closed-loop-reward-hacking-auto-mitigation-v07126) and the [v0.71.26 release notes](https://github.com/MakazhanAlpamys/Soup/releases/tag/v0.71.26).

## What's unproven

Whether the controller **suppresses reward hacking without collapsing true reward** on a realistic setup:

- **7B+ policy** (e.g. Qwen2.5-7B / Llama-3.1-8B) instead of 135M.
- A **real reward model** (trained RM or verifiable-reward task) instead of a synthetic length/sentinel proxy.
- Both `kl_control` (bang-bang) and `pid_lagrangian` controllers, plus the Stage-3 hardening stack.
- **PPO** (currently ships BETA — mechanism unit-tested, on-GPU proof is GRPO-only).

This needs multi-GPU hardware the maintainer doesn't have; it is the honest counterpart to the RTX-3050 proof-of-mechanism limit.

## Proposed validation path

1. Pick a known reward-hackable setup (e.g. a length- or format-exploitable RM on a reasoning/GRPO task).
2. Run a **baseline** (`reward_hack_mitigation: log_only`) and confirm `mitigation_log.jsonl` records the hack onset (drop_pct climbs, completion-length trend diverges).
3. Run `kl_control` and `pid_lagrangian`; measure gamed-proxy reward **and a held-out true-quality metric** across training.
4. Success = the controller bends the gamed proxy back down **while preserving (not collapsing) the held-out true metric** vs. the unmitigated run.
5. Repeat for PPO to graduate it out of BETA.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] ≥1 run on a 7B+ policy with a real reward model where mitigation demonstrably reduces the hacking signal.
- [ ] Held-out true-quality metric does **not** regress materially vs. baseline under mitigation.
- [ ] Both `kl_control` and `pid_lagrangian` exercised; rollback ladder observed to fire at least once.
- [ ] PPO path validated on GPU (removes the BETA caveat) **or** a documented reason it can't be.
- [ ] Findings written up (config + curves) and linked back here.

Community reproduction very welcome — attach your `mitigation_log.jsonl` + curves.

### Feature request


Add two reward functions to `trl.rewards`, both built on existing primitives:

1. **`get_length_scaled_accuracy_reward(alpha=0.5, incorrect_reward=-1.0, reasoning_delimiters=None)`** : a reward-function factory that wraps `reasoning_accuracy_reward` and scales the reward of *correct* completions by their length **relative to the other correct completions of the same prompt** (a z-score within the GRPO group). Implements the length-aware shaping from **GRPO-LEAD** (https://huggingface.co/papers/2504.09696).

2. **`graduated_format_reward(completions, **kwargs)`** : a graduated variant of `think_format_reward` that gives partial credit (`1.0 / 0.5 / 0.25 / 0.0`) for partial `<think>...</think>` structure, providing a denser signal during cold-start training when strict-format matches are rare.


### Motivation


**Length-scaled accuracy : how it differs from the existing `get_cosine_scaled_reward`.**
TRL already has [`get_cosine_scaled_reward`](https://huggingface.co/docs/trl/main/rewards#get_cosine_scaled_reward) (#6066), which also rewards shorter correct completions. The two are complementary, not redundant:

| | `get_cosine_scaled_reward` (existing) | `get_length_scaled_accuracy_reward` (proposed) |
|---|---|---|
| Length reference | **absolute** token count vs a fixed `max_len` budget | **group-relative** z-score among the prompt's correct completions |
| Needs a length budget? | yes (`max_len`) | no — adapts to each prompt's own length distribution |
| Shaping curve | cosine interpolation between fixed bounds | `exp(-alpha * z)`; a group's correct rewards have geometric mean `1.0` |
| Paper | Demystifying Long CoT | GRPO-LEAD |

The group-relative formulation is useful when there is no good global length budget (mixed-difficulty data): on an easy prompt where every completion is short, and on a hard prompt where every completion is long, GRPO-LEAD still applies the same relative pressure toward the shorter correct answers, because it standardizes within the group. A fixed `max_len` schedule cannot do that.

**Graduated format reward.** `think_format_reward` is binary: a completion that emits only `<think>` (or both tags in the wrong order) scores exactly `0.0`, identical to a completion with no tags at all. Early in training that signal is very sparse. A graduated version gives the policy a gradient to climb toward the target structure. Nothing equivalent exists in `trl.rewards` today.

Both functions follow existing conventions: `get_length_scaled_accuracy_reward` mirrors the picklable callable-class factory pattern of `get_cosine_scaled_reward` / `get_soft_overlong_punishment` (so it works under the async GRPO rollout worker), and `graduated_format_reward` sits alongside `think_format_reward`.


### Your contribution

I have an implementation ready (functions, docs, a `paper_index.md` entry for GRPO-LEAD that cross-references the cosine reward, and unit tests including a picklability test) and will open a PR referencing this issue.
title: [Feature] Reasoning reward utilities: group-relative length-scaled accuracy (GRPO-LEAD) + graduated format reward

All observations are against current `main` (986bf86), `bluebird-gymnasium` 0.2.0, in [`bluebird_gymnasium/rewards/expeditious.py`](https://github.com/project-bluebird/BluebirdATC/blob/986bf868da76feda1e2d0f458f03d87dec70544f/bluebird-gymnasium/bluebird_gymnasium/rewards/expeditious.py).

### 1. `expeditious_linear` rewards moving *away* from the exit (sign inverted)

[expeditious.py#L87-L89](https://github.com/project-bluebird/BluebirdATC/blob/986bf868da76feda1e2d0f458f03d87dec70544f/bluebird-gymnasium/bluebird_gymnasium/rewards/expeditious.py#L87-L89):

```python
dist_diff = curr_dist - prev_dist
reward = np.clip(dist_diff, -DIFF_THRESHOLD, DIFF_THRESHOLD)
```

When the aircraft makes progress toward its exit, `curr_dist < prev_dist`, so `dist_diff` is **negative** and the function returns a **negative** reward. This is the opposite of the docstring, which says progress should yield a positive reward up to +1.0. An agent trained with this reward is incentivised to fly away from its sector exit.

**Suggested fix** — negate the difference:

```python
reward = np.clip(-dist_diff, -DIFF_THRESHOLD, DIFF_THRESHOLD)
# or equivalently: dist_diff = prev_dist - curr_dist
```

### 2. `expeditious_quad` has the same inverted sign

[expeditious.py#L150-L153](https://github.com/project-bluebird/BluebirdATC/blob/986bf868da76feda1e2d0f458f03d87dec70544f/bluebird-gymnasium/bluebird_gymnasium/rewards/expeditious.py#L150-L153):

```python
dist_diff = curr_dist - prev_dist
reward = np.clip(dist_diff, -DIFF_THRESHOLD, DIFF_THRESHOLD)
sign = np.sign(reward)
```

`sign` is taken from the raw `dist_diff`, so progress (negative `dist_diff`) again produces a negative final reward, contradicting the docstring. Same fix: negate `dist_diff` (or the final `sign`).

### 3. `expeditious_exp` exponential grows in the wrong direction (and exceeds its documented range)

[expeditious.py#L217-L222](https://github.com/project-bluebird/BluebirdATC/blob/986bf868da76feda1e2d0f458f03d87dec70544f/bluebird-gymnasium/bluebird_gymnasium/rewards/expeditious.py#L217-L222):

```python
if dist_diff < 0:
    dist_diff = max(dist_diff, -DIFF_THRESHOLD)
    # the closer `dist_diff` is to -1.0, the higher the reward
    reward = np.exp(dist_diff + DIFF_THRESHOLD)
```

This one gets the sign convention right (progress → positive reward), but `np.exp(dist_diff + DIFF_THRESHOLD)` is *increasing* in `dist_diff`:

- maximal progress (`dist_diff = -1.0`) → `exp(0) = 1.0`
- minimal progress (`dist_diff → 0⁻`) → `exp(1) ≈ 2.72`

So smaller progress earns a *larger* reward — the opposite of the inline comment and the docstring ("the bigger the difference the closer the reward to 1.0") — and the value can exceed the documented 0.0–1.0 range (before speed scaling). Note `tests/rewards/test_expeditious.py::test_expeditious_exp` asserts `reward <= 1.0`, so this can also cause a test failure depending on the fixture trajectory.

**Suggested fix** — flip the exponent so max progress maps to 1.0:

```python
reward = np.exp(-(dist_diff + DIFF_THRESHOLD))
# dist_diff = -1.0 -> 1.0 ; dist_diff -> 0 -> ~0.37
```

### 4. `expeditious_const` crashes on the first tracked step (missing `else`)

[expeditious.py#L30-L43](https://github.com/project-bluebird/BluebirdATC/blob/986bf868da76feda1e2d0f458f03d87dec70544f/bluebird-gymnasium/bluebird_gymnasium/rewards/expeditious.py#L30-L43):

```python
if prev_ac_tracked_state is None:
    reward = 0.0

if (
    ac_tracked_state.track_dist_to_exit_cr
    < prev_ac_tracked_state.track_dist_to_exit_cr   # AttributeError when None
):
```

When `prev_ac_tracked_state is None` (aircraft tracking just started), `reward` is set to `0.0` but execution falls through to the second `if`, which dereferences `prev_ac_tracked_state` and raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'track_dist_to_exit_cr'`. The other three functions use `else:` correctly here.

**Suggested fix** — change the second `if` to `elif`.

### Note on tests

The tests in `tests/rewards/test_expeditious.py` only assert that the reward falls within the documented range, so they cannot catch the sign inversions in (1) and (2). It may be worth adding direction tests (progress → positive, regression → negative) alongside the fixes.
title: [Bug] expeditious reward functions: inverted sign in linear/quad, wrong-direction exponential in exp, crash in const

## Description

The wallet system should support FAIR rewards as a first-class transaction type so Oxy Rewards distributions can credit users clearly and auditably.

Currently wallet transactions support `deposit`, `withdrawal`, `transfer`, and `purchase`. Rewards should not be hidden as generic deposits because users, admins, and audit flows need to distinguish earned rewards from user deposits or manual transfers.

## Goals

- Add a `reward` transaction type to wallet transactions.
- Credit approved FAIR rewards to the user's Oxy wallet.
- Link reward wallet transactions back to the reward campaign/distribution that generated them.
- Keep reward credits auditable and reversible if needed.
- Avoid immediate on-chain microtransactions; V1 should credit the internal Oxy wallet first.
- Leave withdrawals/on-chain settlement to the existing/future FairCoin withdrawal flow.

## Proposed transaction changes

Extend transaction type:

```ts
TransactionType = "deposit" | "withdrawal" | "transfer" | "purchase" | "reward";
```

Add optional reward metadata:

```ts
Transaction {
  _id: ObjectId;
  userId: ObjectId;
  type: "reward";
  amount: number;
  status: "pending" | "completed" | "failed" | "cancelled" | "reversed";

  rewardCampaignId?: ObjectId;
  rewardApplicationId?: ObjectId;
  rewardDistributionId?: ObjectId;

  asset?: "FAIR";
  description?: string;
  externalReference?: string;

  completedAt?: Date;
  createdAt: Date;
  updatedAt: Date;
}
```

## Crediting behavior

When a reward distribution is approved:

1. Create a `Transaction` with `type: "reward"`.
2. Link it to the reward campaign/application/distribution.
3. Increment the user's wallet balance atomically.
4. Mark the reward distribution as `credited`.
5. Return the wallet transaction ID for audit/history.

## Reversal behavior

If a reward was issued incorrectly:

- Do not silently delete the original transaction.
- Create a reversal/adjustment transaction or mark the reward transaction as reversed, depending on the final wallet ledger design.
- Update wallet balance safely.
- Preserve auditability.

## UI/API behavior

- User transaction history should show reward transactions distinctly.
- Reward transactions should display the campaign name/source when available.
- Admin tooling should be able to trace a wallet reward back to the reward campaign and distribution.

## Dependencies

Related to:

- #221 reputation-gated FAIR reward pools
- #217 reputation transaction ledger

## Acceptance criteria

- Wallet transaction schema supports `reward`.
- Reward credits are atomic with wallet balance updates.
- Reward transactions link to reward distribution/campaign records.
- Reward transactions appear correctly in user transaction history.
- Reward credits can be audited and reversed/adjusted if necessary.
- Tests cover successful reward crediting, insufficient/invalid distribution state, duplicate credit prevention, and transaction history display.
title: [IMPROVEMENT] Add wallet reward transaction type and FAIR reward crediting flow

## Motivation
`UTXOSet.validate(transaction:)` in `Sources/UTXOChain/UTXOSet.swift` (lines 45-48) short-circuits and returns `nil` for **any** coinbase transaction without checking the output amount:

```swift
if tx.isCoinbase {
    return nil
}
```

This means a coinbase can mint an arbitrary amount — there is no cap tying it to `Miner.reward` plus collected fees. This is a consensus-breaking money-printing bug: a crafted block whose coinbase pays 1_000_000 passes `validate` and `Blockchain.validateChain` (`Sources/UTXOChain/Chain.swift`).

## Proposed change
- Pass the expected reward + total fees of the block into validation and reject a coinbase whose output sum exceeds it.
- Since `UTXOSet.validate` is per-transaction, add block-level coinbase validation inside `Blockchain.validateChain` (`Chain.swift` lines 105-111): compute the sum of (inputSum - outputSum) fees across non-coinbase txs and assert the coinbase output sum <= `miner.reward` + fees.
- Reject blocks containing more than one coinbase transaction.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A coinbase paying more than `reward + fees` is rejected by `validateChain`.
- [ ] A block with two coinbase txs is rejected.
- [ ] New test in `Tests/UTXOChainTests/UTXOChainTests.swift` covering over-reward coinbase.
- [ ] Existing tests still pass.
title: [correctness] Validate coinbase reward and fees in UTXOSet.validate

body:
## Motivation

verl-omni's reward framework supports two reward model pathways:

- **DisRM** (discriminative): text-only, subject to floating-point nondeterminism, **cannot handle visual input**
- **GenRM** (generative): supports VLM Vision API, but **sampling params hardcoded** (`temperature=0.7, top_p=0.8`) in every `/v1/chat/completions` request, with no seed control for reproducibility

Three gaps:

1. **No floating-point determinism** — flash attention split-K, CUDA matmul, NCCL all-reduce, MoE routing can all produce floating-point variation across RM inference runs
2. **No configurable GenRM sampling** — GenRM's hardcoded per-request params bypass RM rollout config; users cannot control sampling behavior or provide seed for reproducibility
3. **No VLM scoring path** — enabling RM without a custom reward function has no built-in visual scoring entry point, requiring manual configuration

## Design

Add `deterministic` and `seed` fields under `reward_model` in YAML config:

- **`deterministic=true`** — full determinism applied to RM actors via `enable_full_determinism(seed)` + `PYTHONHASHSEED` injected via `runtime_env`; `seed` propagated to GenRM HTTP requests (same seed + same input → same output, controlled pseudorandom)
- **`deterministic=false`** — full randomness, `seed` not propagated
- **Sampling params** (`temperature/do_sample/top_k/top_p`) are entirely user-configured in YAML under `rollout`, the `deterministic` flag does not override them

### 1. Floating-point determinism

RM inference uses `name=vllm` servers (`vLLMReplica` + `vLLMHttpServer`). When `deterministic=true`, monkey-patch `vLLMReplica.launch_servers()` with `_DeterministicServerProxy` which does two things:

**Env vars injection** — `PYTHONHASHSEED` must be set before Python process startup, so it is injected into RM actor `runtime_env`. Rollout actors remain unaffected (`is_reward_model` guard).

**Server class swap** — Replace `vLLMHttpServer` with `_DeterministicRMHttpServer(vLLMHttpServer)` subclass, which calls verl's `enable_full_determinism(seed)` in `_post_init`. This covers all in-process determinism: env vars (`CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CONFIG`, `FLASH_ATTENTION_DETERMINISTIC`, `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT`, `NCCL_LAUNCH_MODE`, `NCCL_PROTO`), Python/NumPy/PyTorch seeds, deterministic algorithms, cuDNN config.

| Setting | Set by |
|---|---|
| `PYTHONHASHSEED=str(seed)` | `runtime_env` (before process startup) |
| `CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CONFIG=:16:8` | `enable_full_determinism` (in-process) |
| `FLASH_ATTENTION_DETERMINISTIC=1` | `enable_full_determinism` (in-process) |
| `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1` | `enable_full_determinism` (in-process) |
| `NCCL_LAUNCH_MODE=GROUP` | `enable_full_determinism` (in-process) |
| `NCCL_PROTO=Simple` | `enable_full_determinism` (in-process) |
| `random.seed(seed)` | `enable_full_determinism` (in-process) |
| `np.random.seed(seed)` | `enable_full_determinism` (in-process) |
| `torch.manual_seed(seed)` | `enable_full_determinism` (in-process) |
| `torch.cuda.manual_seed_all(seed)` | `enable_full_determinism` (in-process) |
| `torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True, warn_only=True)` | `enable_full_determinism` (in-process) |
| `cudnn.deterministic=True, benchmark=False, enabled=False` | `enable_full_determinism` (in-process) |

### 2. Configurable GenRM sampling + seed control

`VisualRewardManager` passes RM rollout config sampling params to `compute_score_ocr` via `sampling_params` kwarg, replacing hardcoded `DEFAULT_SAMPLING_PARAMS`. When `deterministic=true`, `seed` (from `reward_model.seed`) is included in `sampling_params` and propagates to vLLM's `/v1/chat/completions` request. When `deterministic=false`, `seed` is excluded — full randomness.

Sampling params (`temperature/do_sample/top_k/top_p`) are user-configured. Examples:
- `temperature=0, top_p=1.0` → greedy, fully deterministic
- `temperature>0, seed=42` → controlled pseudorandom, reproducible

### 3. VLM scoring path

When RM enabled + no `custom_reward_function.path`, auto-set path to `compute_score_ocr`. This provides the GenRM scoring entry point needed for VLM visual scoring.

### Propagation chain

```
reward.yaml (deterministic: true/false, seed: 42, rollout.temperature/do_sample/top_k/top_p)
  → DiffusionRayTrainer._init_online_rollout_stack()
      ├─ deterministic=true: monkey-patch vLLMReplica → _DeterministicServerProxy
      │     ├─ inject PYTHONHASHSEED into runtime_env
      │     └─ swap server_class → _DeterministicRMHttpServer (calls enable_full_determinism in _post_init)
      ├─ RM enabled + no custom_reward_function: auto-set → compute_score_ocr
  → VisualRewardManager
      ├─ sampling_params from rollout config (temperature, do_sample, top_k, top_p)
      ├─ deterministic=true: include seed from reward_model.seed
      ├─ deterministic=false: exclude seed
      → compute_score_ocr(sampling_params=...)
          → HTTP /v1/chat/completions request uses user-configured params
```

---

## Changes

### 1. YAML config

**File**: `verl_omni/trainer/config/reward/reward.yaml`

Add `deterministic: false` and `seed: 42` under `reward_model`.

### 2. Floating-point determinism

**File**: `verl_omni/trainer/diffusion/ray_diffusion_trainer.py`

Define `_DeterministicRMHttpServer(vLLMHttpServer)` subclass. When `deterministic=true` + RM enabled, monkey-patch `vLLMReplica` with `_reward_deterministic` class attribute and `launch_servers()` override via `_DeterministicServerProxy`. `_DeterministicServerProxy` injects `PYTHONHASHSEED` into RM actor `runtime_env` and swaps `self.server_class` to `_DeterministicRMHttpServer`.

**File**: `verl_omni/workers/rollout/vllm_rollout/vllm_omni_async_server.py`

Remove `_DETERMINISTIC_RM_ENV_VARS` static dict.

### 3. Configurable GenRM sampling + seed control

**File**: `verl_omni/reward_loop/reward_manager/visual.py`

Pass `sampling_params` from RM rollout config. Include `seed` when `deterministic=true`, exclude when `deterministic=false`.

**File**: `verl_omni/utils/reward_score/genrm_ocr.py`

Add `sampling_params: dict = None` parameter. Use `sampling_params or DEFAULT_SAMPLING_PARAMS` in HTTP request.

---

## Backward Compatibility

- `deterministic=true` affects RM actors only; rollout unaffected
- `deterministic=false` preserves existing behavior
- `sampling_params` defaults to `None`; when `None`, `DEFAULT_SAMPLING_PARAMS` used
- `custom_reward_function` auto-set when RM enabled + no path provided

## Verification

1. `deterministic=true`: `PYTHONHASHSEED` injected via runtime_env + `enable_full_determinism(seed)` called in `_post_init`
2. Rollout actors unaffected (`is_reward_model` guard)
3. `deterministic=true` + `seed=42`: reproducible GenRM scores
4. `deterministic=false`: existing behavior

## Files

| File | Change |
|---|---|
| `verl_omni/trainer/config/reward/reward.yaml` | Add `deterministic: false` and `seed: 42` under `reward_model` |
| `verl_omni/trainer/diffusion/ray_diffusion_trainer.py` | `_DeterministicRMHttpServer` + monkey-patch `vLLMReplica` |
| `verl_omni/workers/rollout/vllm_rollout/vllm_omni_async_server.py` | Remove `_DETERMINISTIC_RM_ENV_VARS` |
| `verl_omni/reward_loop/reward_manager/visual.py` | Pass `sampling_params`; include/exclude `seed` |
| `verl_omni/utils/reward_score/genrm_ocr.py` | Add `sampling_params` param |
| `tests/reward_loop/test_visual_reward_manager.py` | `test_deterministic_reward_reproducibility` |

**Severity:** Low · **Confidence:** Confirmed (demonstrated by test) · Part of #892 · Elevated from round-1 informational, demonstrated in round-3 invariant tests

**Location:** `LibInteractionRewards.poolRemaining` / `getInteractionPoolRemaining()` (pure accounting: 69M cap − paidOut); borrower-LIF `vpfiHeld` custody + `rebateAmount` in `LibVPFIDiscount` / `ClaimFacet`; all share the single Diamond VPFI ERC20 balance. Demonstration: `contracts/test/audit/Round3CrossFacetInvariants.t.sol::test_Invariant_VpfiCustody_InteractionPoolAccountingIsNotBacked`

### Description
The Diamond's VPFI balance backs multiple independent accounting buckets — interaction-reward pool payouts, borrower-LIF custody (`vpfiHeld`), borrower rebates (`rebateAmount`), and keeper/reward budgets — segregated only by independent counters. `getInteractionPoolRemaining()` is pure accounting (cap − paidOut) with **no dedicated backing** and is paid from the same balance as LIF custody/rebates. There is no on-chain invariant asserting `VPFI.balanceOf(diamond) ≥ Σ vpfiHeld + Σ rebateAmount + poolRemaining + budgets`.

The round-3 invariant suite includes two tests here:
- `test_Invariant_VpfiCustody_DiamondBalanceCoversHardObligations` asserts `balanceOf(diamond) ≥ Σ vpfiHeld + Σ rebateAmount` (the *hard* custody obligations) — expected to pass.
- `test_Invariant_VpfiCustody_InteractionPoolAccountingIsNotBacked` asserts `balanceOf(diamond) < hard obligations + poolRemaining` — **this test passing IS the finding**: the reward pool's "remaining" is not separately funded.

### Attack scenario / impact
Not an external exploit — an operational/solvency risk. If the interaction pool is ever under-seeded (operator does not deposit the full emission schedule up front) or reward payouts run ahead of deposits, reward claims can draw down VPFI that is earmarked as `vpfiHeld` custody or `rebateAmount`, surfacing later as a **revert when a borrower tries to claim their rebate** (first-come-first-served insolvency between reward claimants and custody/rebate claimants). Silent until the balance is actually short.

### Recommendation
1. Add a monitored on-chain view (`getTotalVpfiCustody()` + pool/budget totals) and, ideally, a hard invariant assertion that `balanceOf(diamond) ≥ Σ all obligations` at the fund-moving boundaries.
2. Document the funding requirement at deploy (seed the full pool up front) and gate reward payouts on backed balance.
3. **Missing view helpers** flagged by the invariant tests (add these to make the invariant cheaply assertable): `getTotalVpfiCustody()` (avoid O(n) loan-walk), `previewPreclose()` fee/interest decomposition, cheap loan-id-by-status enumeration, and a liquidation-entitlement breakdown view. These also unblock the deferred invariant-test scaffold noted in `docs/AuditIntake.md`.

Related: #919 (reward cap fail-open), #895 (permissionless sweep).

**Symptom.** Eligible Trials haben `overfit_gap = 0`, d. h. `is_sortino_median ≤ base(=5)`. Der annualisierte OOS-Sortino (≥5, geklemmt) liegt **über** dem IS-Median — ein Muster, das typisch für ein **glückliches OOS-Sub-Fenster** ist und auf dem Holdout revertiert (`R_symbol ≈ −5.1`). Die Reward-Funktion gibt dafür **vollen Kredit**.

**Root-Cause (Mathematik).** `overfit_gap = max(0, is_sortino_median − base)` bestraft ausschließlich `IS > OOS`. Der Fall `OOS ≫ IS` (Overfit auf ein günstiges Fenster) wird mit `gap = 0` **nicht** bestraft. Zusätzlich fließt in den Reward der **gepoolte/Median-** OOS-Sortino, nicht die **Streuung** über die Folds — ein einzelner starker Fold kann den Wert tragen (die Fold-Konsistenz greift nur im Gate über `oos_min_profitable_folds_frac`, nicht im Reward).

**Fix.**
1. **Symmetrische Divergenz-Strafe** statt einseitigem Overfit-Gap:
   ```
   divergence_pen = w_of · |is_sortino_median − base|
   ```
   Ein großer Betrag in *beide* Richtungen signalisiert Instabilität IS↔OOS. Optional asymmetrisch gewichtet (`OOS≫IS` etwas milder, aber ungleich 0).
2. **Fold-Dispersions-Strafe** in den Reward heben: Streuung der Per-Fold-OOS-Sortinos (`collect_oos_fold_sortinos` existiert bereits, `backtest_runner.py:816`) als Malus:
   ```
   reward −= w_disp · pstdev(per_fold_oos_sortino)
   ```
   Belohnt *konsistente* statt *glücklicher* Performance und ist die Reward-seitige Ergänzung zum Gate-seitigen #550.
3. **Deflated Sortino** (#553, aktuell `deflated_selection=false`) als Winner-Kriterium aktivieren (siehe #568): kontrolliert die False-Positive-Winner-Rate gegen das Rausch-Maximum über N Konfigurationen — genau der Selection-Bias, der hier zuschlägt.

**Akzeptanzkriterien.**
- Property-Test: bei `OOS_sortino = 5`, `IS_median = 1` ist `reward` messbar niedriger als bei `OOS = IS = 5` (OOS-Glück wird bestraft).
- Fold-Dispersion wirkt: zwei Trials mit gleichem Median-OOS-Sortino, aber unterschiedlicher Fold-Streuung, erhalten unterschiedlichen Reward (niedrigere Streuung → höher).
- A/B auf `TSLA.ETORO`: mittlerer Holdout-Regret sinkt gegenüber Baseline.

**Betroffene Dateien.** `automation/optimizer/reward.py` (`compute_reward` — `divergence_pen`, `fold_dispersion_pen`), `automation/optimizer/parsing.py` (Fold-Sortino-Streuung in `TournamentMetrics` durchreichen, falls nicht vorhanden), `automation/tests/test_issue_566_overfit_symmetry.py` (neu).

## Context

`compute_reward_payout` calculates each winner's pro-rata share of `market.reward_amount`. The
platform whitelists arbitrary SPL mints; large-supply / low-decimal tokens can produce very large
`reward_amount` and per-user `score` values (score ≤ stake amount ≤ u64::MAX).

## Problem

The reward is computed multiply-before-divide in u128:

```rust
// claim_rewards.rs — compute_reward_payout
let reward = (user_score as u128)
    .checked_mul(market.reward_amount as u128)
    .ok_or(ErrorCode::Overflow)?
    .checked_mul(option.reward_bp as u128)
    .ok_or(ErrorCode::Overflow)?
    .checked_div(
        total_score.checked_mul(active_bp as u128).ok_or(ErrorCode::Overflow)?,
    )
    .ok_or(ErrorCode::Overflow)? as u64;
```

`user_score * reward_amount` alone can reach ~`u64::MAX² ≈ u128::MAX`; multiplying by
`reward_bp` (up to 10_000) can overflow u128 before the division that would have produced a
result ≤ `reward_amount`.

## Theoretical reachability

Not adversarial — configuration + token supply dependent. Example: if
`user_score * reward_amount > u128::MAX / 10_000 ≈ 3.4×10³⁴`, the second `checked_mul` returns
`Overflow` and `claim_rewards` reverts permanently for that winner.

Whether this is reachable in practice for realistic token decimals/supply is **unverified** —
needs a test.

## Impact

If reachable: winning staker's payout permanently unclaimable; `close_stake_account` also blocked
for scored winners → reward + fee refund + rent frozen.

## Suggested directions

1. **First: add a test** (in `score.rs` unit tests or `claim_rewards` tests) that either:
   - demonstrates overflow at realistic/large token parameters, or
   - proves the intermediate product stays below `u128::MAX` under documented bounds.
2. **If confirmed reachable**: reorder to divide before the final multiply:

```rust
let base = (user_score as u128)
    .checked_mul(market.reward_amount as u128).ok_or(Overflow)?
    .checked_div(total_score).ok_or(Overflow)?;  // ≤ reward_amount
let reward = base
    .checked_mul(option.reward_bp as u128).ok_or(Overflow)?
    .checked_div(active_bp as u128).ok_or(Overflow)? as u64;
```

Still floors, still ≤ pool. Requires `total_score > 0` (see zero-total-score issue).

Move advancement-backed event IDs and event reward-function references onto Sand's typed resource-location / function-reference APIs instead of accepting bare strings on the normal event authoring path.

## Problem

Verified against current `main`, the open issue list, recent PRs, and `docs/typedness-audit.md`:

- The typedness audit still classifies `sand-core/event/mod.rs` as only **Mostly typed** because `EventAdvancement`/event IDs are raw strings and should use `ResourceLocation`.
- `sand-core/src/event/mod.rs` models `EventId::Explicit(&'static str)` and `EventId::resolve(...) -> String`, so invalid resource locations can remain in the event configuration until a later command/export boundary.
- `sand-core/src/event/builder.rs` exposes `EventBuilder::id(id: impl Into<String>)`, then leaks the string into `EventId::Explicit(...)`; this is not a typed boundary and makes invalid IDs look like normal API usage.
- `EventConfig::advancement(advancement_id: impl Into<String>, reward_fn: impl Into<String>)` parses the advancement ID internally but still accepts raw string inputs, and forwards `reward_fn` into `AdvancementRewards::function(...)` as a raw function reference.
- #183 covers the general advancement component surface for display/icon/rewards/parent IDs, but it does not explicitly cover the event builder API that generates advancement-backed event components.
- #194 covers typed function macro arguments; it is related to function calls/macros but does not type event reward function references.

For a strongly typed event framework, normal event authoring should not allow malformed advancement IDs or reward function IDs to travel as arbitrary strings.

## Suggested design

- Replace or supplement `EventId::Explicit(&'static str)` with a typed resource-location-backed form, for example `EventId::Explicit(ResourceLocation)` or `EventId::Explicit(AdvancementId)` if a dedicated advancement ID wrapper exists.
- Add typed constructors such as:
  - `EventId::explicit(id: impl TryInto<ResourceLocation>) -> Result<Self, ...>` or a panicking `new` plus fallible `try_explicit` depending on existing Sand conventions.
  - `EventBuilder::id(ResourceLocation)` / `EventBuilder::advancement_id(...)` with a clearly named raw/custom escape hatch only if needed.
- Update `EventConfig::advancement(...)` so the advancement ID and reward function argument use typed resource/function reference types on the normal path, reusing `ResourceLocation`, `FunctionRef`, or `IntoFunctionRef` rather than `impl Into<String>`.
- Keep compatibility shims if needed, but make them visibly deprecated or raw so new users and agents choose the typed API.
- Ensure #183's advancement reward typing and this event-specific builder work agree on the same function-reference type.

## Acceptance criteria

- Event builder APIs expose typed advancement IDs and typed reward-function references for normal usage.
- Invalid event advancement IDs fail at the Sand boundary with an actionable diagnostic instead of silently becoming malformed advancement/revoke commands.
- Invalid reward function references used by event advancements fail before JSON/function output is written.
- Existing `EventId::Auto` behavior remains stable and still resolves from namespace + handler path.
- Raw/custom escape hatches, if retained, are explicit in naming and documentation.
- Docs/examples for `AdvancementEvent`, `EventBuilder`, and `EventConfig::advancement(...)` show the typed path.

## Test expectations

- Unit tests in `sand-core/src/event/` for valid typed explicit IDs, invalid explicit IDs, and stable `EventId::Auto` output.
- Regression tests proving `EventConfig::advancement(...)` emits the same valid JSON for typed IDs/function refs as before.
- Negative tests for malformed advancement IDs and malformed reward function IDs.
- If export-level validation already has a shared component validation path, add one test proving a bad event advancement cannot be written as malformed datapack output.

## Risks

- This may touch older examples or compatibility call sites that pass plain strings; keep a migration path or deprecated shim if the breakage is too large.
- Coordinate with #183 so `AdvancementRewards::function(...)` and event reward-function references do not grow two incompatible function ID types.
- Coordinate with #194 so typed function references still work once function macros / `function ... with ...` support grows.

## Roadmap priority

Medium-high. This is smaller than the broad advancement trigger rewrite, but it sits directly on the public event API and affects the same typed Rust datapack authoring promise as the current advancement/event roadmap.

## References

- `docs/typedness-audit.md` event section and Phase 6 migration note.
- `sand-core/src/event/mod.rs`
- `sand-core/src/event/builder.rs`
- Related: #183

## Context
Non-blocking future-watch surfaced by S4 (#23) code review. The recall transform now does **fuse-then-rerank**: `rrfFuse`(semantic, structural) → S1 exclusion → `rerankByReward` → top-N. `rerankByReward` (sub-epic ①, #11) sorts by raw per-page `baseScore × rewardFactor`. Because RRF produces a *rank-based* consensus order (not a comparable magnitude), a subsequent sort on raw `baseScore` can partially **undo** the fused rank order.

## Why it's dormant today
`SHIPPED_REWARD_MODE='shadow'` → `rewardFactor` is forced neutral and `rerankByReward` is effectively identity, so fuse-then-rerank preserves the RRF order. **No live impact now.** This only bites when the reward mode is flipped to LIVE (the gated, deferred ① flip — needs the real-data lift gate + operator ratification).

Revisit the interaction so reward re-rank composes with RRF rather than overriding it — e.g. fold the reward factor INTO the RRF score (rank-aware), or re-rank within RRF-rank bands, rather than a raw-magnitude sort over the fused set. Add a test that a fused order is not inverted by a live reward factor.

body:
## Problem Statement

Miles trains coding agents with RLVR (Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards): the agent edits a repository inside a Harbor Trial, the task's test suite runs, and the reward is 1.0 if the tests pass, 0.0 otherwise. Today, for the SWE-style adapters used in RL training, grading happens **in the same container the agent worked in** (shared verifier mode).

"Verifiable" is not "un-gameable." RL relentlessly optimizes whatever is measured, so a capable policy discovers that the lazy way to make tests pass is not to fix the bug but to tamper with the grading machinery itself: delete or edit the failing test, hard-code the expected output, patch the test harness to always exit 0, or forge the reward file directly. Once found, the policy learns the exploit instead of the skill — and this failure mode gets *worse* as the model gets more capable, which is exactly what makes the training stack unsafe to scale.

As the engineer running these training jobs, I cannot currently trust the reward signal: a rising training reward may mean the policy is getting better at software engineering, or better at cheating. Heuristic detection (scanning diffs for suspicious commands) is an arms race the policy eventually wins.

## Solution

Port slime's **no-test-cheating guarantee** into the Harbor Miles fork: a *structural* defense in which the agent physically cannot touch the thing that grades it.

Two sandboxes, one trust boundary:

- **Work sandbox** — the agent acts here with full permissions. The framework (never the agent) captures its work as a **git diff** with scaffolding excluded. That diff is the *only* artifact that crosses the boundary.
- **Eval sandbox** — a fresh, clean container booted from the same task image at the same base commit. Nobody but the grader runs here. It defensively applies the diff (three escalating strategies; if none apply, reward is 0.0), then runs the **dataset-owned** test harness and grades all-or-nothing: reward 1.0 only if every required test (`fail_to_pass` ∪ `pass_to_pass`) passes.

Whatever the agent did to its own sandbox — deleted tests, patched conftest, forged reward files — never existed in the eval sandbox. The defense is isolation by construction, not detection.

The guarantee is **default-on for the Miles training path**: the protected task templates are regenerated, and the Miles agent server refuses (behind a default-on flag) to run tasks that lack the protection, so a stale task directory cannot silently reopen the cheating surface.

## User Stories

1. As a Miles RL engineer, I want the reward computed in a clean sandbox the agent never touched, so that reward-hacking by grader tampering is impossible by construction rather than merely detected.
2. As a Miles RL engineer, I want the only artifact crossing from work sandbox to eval sandbox to be a framework-captured git diff, so that the agent cannot smuggle a tampered grader, a forged reward file, or any other state across the trust boundary.
3. As a Miles RL engineer, I want the diff captured by the Trial itself rather than written by the agent, so that a policy cannot fabricate its own submission.
4. As a Miles RL engineer, I want scaffolding files (problem statements, trajectory logs, agent runner scripts) excluded from the captured diff via pathspec exclusions, so that non-solution files never pollute the graded change.
5. As a Miles RL engineer, I want the diff taken against the task's base commit rather than the current HEAD, so that an agent running `git commit` or `git checkout` cannot blank out or redirect its submission.
6. As a Miles RL engineer, I want the eval sandbox booted from the same task image at the same base commit as the work sandbox, so that the diff applies to an identical baseline and honest work is not zeroed by baseline drift.
7. As a Miles RL engineer, I want a defensive three-strategy patch application (3-way merge, then plain apply, then patch fallback), so that cosmetic whitespace or context differences do not discard genuinely correct solutions.
8. As a Miles RL engineer, I want "diff won't apply" to produce reward 0.0 with an `applied_cleanly = 0` signal — never a crash — so that malformed submissions fail closed and remain diagnosable.
9. As a Miles RL engineer, I want won't-apply rollouts kept in the training batch with reward 0.0 by default (matching the slime reference behavior), so that v1 is faithful to the proven design, while the emitted `applied_cleanly` signal lets me switch to masking with a one-line trainer-side filter change later.
10. As a Miles RL engineer, I want grading to be all-or-nothing over the dataset's `fail_to_pass` and `pass_to_pass` sets, so that partial fixes and fixes that regress existing behavior never earn reward.
11. As a Miles RL engineer, I want the agent's own in-sandbox test run to never be read for reward, so that "it passed locally" counts for nothing.
12. As a Miles RL engineer, I want the reward's companion signals (`solved`, `applied_cleanly`) delivered in the eval report alongside the scalar reward, so that GRPO advantage computation and sampling filters can use them with no new plumbing.
13. As a Miles RL engineer, I want the verifier result to carry only numeric values, so that a successful solve can never crash reward parsing and silently destroy my positive training signal.
14. As a Miles RL engineer, I want apply-strategy and failure-reason diagnostics recorded in a report artifact rather than the reward mapping, so that I can monitor real-world apply-failure rates without breaking the typed reward contract.
15. As an agent-server operator, I want the server to refuse, by default, any task that does not resolve to the protected configuration, so that a stale task directory on a training node fails loudly instead of training on gameable rewards.
16. As an agent-server operator, I want that enforcement behind a flag that defaults to on in the Miles launch scripts, so that non-SWE experiments can opt out deliberately but never accidentally.
17. As a benchmark adapter maintainer, I want the swe-rebench-v2 and swegym task templates regenerated with separate verifier mode plus submission capture, so that every newly generated task is protected without per-task effort.
18. As a benchmark adapter maintainer, I want the verifier image to bundle the test script and grading configuration at image-build time, so that the grader is dataset-owned and immutable from the agent's perspective.
19. As a benchmark adapter maintainer, I want the eval environment to run with networking disabled by default, so that a poisoned diff cannot fetch dependencies or exfiltrate data during grading.
20. As a Harbor task author, I want the submission-capture block to be optional configuration that defaults to absent, so that every existing task behaves exactly as before this feature.
21. As a developer on this fork, I want a permanent probe suite — oracle agent scores 1.0, nop agent scores 0.0, cheating agent scores 0.0 — so that the guarantee is continuously proven by tests, not assumed.
22. As a developer on this fork, I want a conftest-poisoning probe that demonstrates the known residual hole, so that the accepted limitation stays visible and regression-tracked instead of forgotten.
23. As a developer on this fork, I want the probe agents to be fully scripted (no LLM, no external binaries), so that the Docker proofs run on an Apple-Silicon laptop under x86 emulation.
24. As a developer on this fork, I want fast mocked unit tests covering capture ordering, template rendering, and server refusal, so that the no-Docker test suite protects the feature on every change.
25. As a future contributor, I want the core-framework change confined to one new seam with a small interface, so that review stays tractable and upstreaming later remains possible.

## Implementation Decisions

**Threat model and claim scope.** The guarantee covers grader tampering, reward-file forgery, and test deletion/modification inside the work sandbox — those become impossible by construction. One residual is explicitly accepted in v1: a diff that carries a malicious harness-config file (e.g. a repo-root `conftest.py`) can still influence the test run inside the eval sandbox, because the harness resets only the dataset's listed test files. slime has the same residual. It is documented, demonstrated by a probe, and out of scope to fix. All claims in docs must be scoped to "grader tampering is impossible," not "cheating is impossible."

**One new seam.** The only new framework seam is a Trial-owned submission-capture step that runs after the agent finishes and before artifacts are collected, gated by a new optional submission block in the task's verifier configuration. When the block is absent, behavior is byte-for-byte today's. Shape of the config contract (from the design workflow):

```toml
[verifier]
environment_mode = "separate"

[verifier.submission]          # new, optional; absence = no capture
workdir = "/testbed"           # repo root inside the work sandbox
path = "agent.patch"           # artifact name the eval side consumes
exclude = ["PROBLEM_STATEMENT.md", "*.trajectory.json"]  # pathspec exclusions

[verifier.environment]
network_mode = "no-network"
```

**Capture semantics.** The capture is executed by the framework in the still-live work sandbox: intent-to-add staging so new untracked files appear as additions, diff taken against the task's base commit (not bare HEAD), pathspec exclusions for scaffolding, git safe-directory handling for non-root users. The output lands in the conventional artifact directory so the existing artifact pipeline transports it into the eval sandbox with zero new transport code.

**Boundary transport and contract.** The whole artifact directory technically crosses (existing pipeline behavior); the grading script's contract is to consume only the captured patch. The eval sandbox's reward directory is wiped by the existing machinery before grading, so agent-planted reward files are destroyed.

**Eval sandbox.** Realized by Harbor's existing separate verifier mode: the work container is stopped, then a fresh verifier container boots from an image built on the same per-instance task image (so the repository is already a clean base-commit checkout — baseline alignment by image identity). The verifier image must explicitly bundle the test script and grading config at build time; verifier mode is resolved from the task definition, not the per-run request, so the mode switch lives in the adapter template.

**Defensive apply (in the adapter's grading script, before the dataset's own test-file reset).** Three escalating strategies: 3-way git apply, plain git apply, then patch fallback. If all fail, the script writes a numeric fail-closed reward and exits successfully. An empty diff is a clean no-op. Reward file contract (from the design workflow; numeric-only is load-bearing):

```json
{"reward": 0.0, "solved": 0, "applied_cleanly": 0}
```

String diagnostics (which apply strategy succeeded, failure reason) go to a separate report artifact, never into the reward mapping — the verifier result's reward type accepts only numbers, and a string value would crash validation on the success path.

**Grading.** Reuses the adapters' existing all-or-nothing evaluation: required = `fail_to_pass` ∪ `pass_to_pass`, solved iff every required test passes, no partial credit. Grading config is baked into the verifier image (dataset-owned).

**Reward policy.** Default is zero-and-keep (slime-faithful): a won't-apply rollout scores 0.0 and stays in the batch. `applied_cleanly` rides the eval report to the trainer so masking becomes a trainer-side filter tunable later; trainer-side consumers must read it as 0/1, not a boolean.

**Enforcement (default-on).** The Miles agent server gains a require-anticheat flag, default on in the Miles launch scripts, that refuses to run tasks not resolving to separate mode with a submission block. All swe-rebench-v2 and swegym task directories are regenerated with the new templates.

**Verifier selection.** v1 uses the stock Harbor verifier only — no custom verifier import path. This deliberately sidesteps a confirmed bug where custom verifiers in separate mode lose the tests-upload suppression flag.

**Provenance.** Design produced by a multi-agent design workflow (three options, each adversarially verified against the fork's actual code), then sharpened in a grilling session on 2026-07-03 that locked: scope, zero-and-keep default, accepted conftest residual, Mac-based proofs, probe-suite acceptance, default-on enforcement, fork-only delivery.

## Testing Decisions

**What makes a good test here:** assert external behavior at the seams — reward values, artifact contracts, refusal responses, rendered template content — never internals. Given a submission config, the capture step emits the contracted git command and artifact; given a rendered template, the grading script contains the three-strategy escalation and the fail-closed branch; given an unprotected task, the server refuses; given real containers, the end-to-end rewards match expectations.

**Fast suite (no Docker), runs on every change:**
- Capture: mocked environment records the executed command; assert intent-to-add, base-commit-relative diff, every exclusion pathspec, artifact destination, no-op when the config block is absent, and ordering (capture strictly before artifact collection).
- Templates: pure string assertions on the rendered grading script (escalation order, fail-closed numeric reward, exit-zero) and on the rendered task definition (separate mode, submission block, no-network verifier environment).
- Reward contract: a sample numeric reward file round-trips into the verifier result and out through the agent server's reward extraction, with `solved`/`applied_cleanly` arriving in the eval report.
- Enforcement: agent server refuses a task resolving to shared mode when the flag is on; accepts when off.
- Prior art: the existing mocked Miles agent-server unit suite (async-mock based, no Docker) is the pattern to follow; the 2870-passing unit baseline must stay green.

**Acceptance suite (Docker, slow-marked, permanent).** This is the definition of done, run on Mac + Colima with scripted agents:
- Oracle agent (applies the gold patch) → reward 1.0, solved, applied cleanly. Proves reward is honestly earnable end-to-end and baselines align.
- Nop agent (no edits) → empty diff applies as no-op, required tests fail, reward 0.0 without any crash.
- Cheating-probe agent (deletes tests, rewrites conftest to exit 0, plants a fake reward file) → reward 0.0. The regression that proves the structural guarantee.
- Conftest-poisoning probe → documents the accepted residual by demonstrating it (expected-failure style, tracked, not hidden).
- Prior art: existing slow/runtime-marked Docker tests in the fork; the oracle and nop agents already exist as fixtures.

## Out of Scope

- All adapters other than swe-rebench-v2 and swegym (classic swebench, multi-swe-bench, swebenchpro, and the ~80 others).
- Multi-step trials (v1 is single-step; the target adapters are single-step).
- The two-phase orchestration variant in the Miles bridge (work trial → eval trial) — a later layer on top of this work.
- A custom diff-eval verifier module — kept in reserve; v1 uses the stock verifier.
- Fixing the conftest-poisoning residual (accepted, documented, probed).
- Implementing the trainer-side masking filter in Miles (the signal is emitted; the filter remains a later one-line tunable).
- Grading of binary build artifacts (a text diff cannot carry them; the target datasets don't need them).
- Any heuristic cheat *detection* (diff scanning, command classifiers) — explicitly rejected in favor of structure.
- Upstreaming to harbor-framework/harbor (fork-only for now; the small core seam keeps the option open).

## Further Notes

- **Reference implementation:** slime's coding-agent RL example (the `git_diff` capture, `evaluate` with clean-sandbox boot, `_apply_diff` escalation, and required-subset grading) is the ground truth this ports. The wiki mirror in the `harbor_primeIntellect_smileAgent` vault holds a read-only copy.
- **Cost model:** two container boots per attempt plus a clean test run (~minutes on the tail). This is slime's published tradeoff; Miles's fully-async training absorbs the latency. The agent-server concurrency slot is held roughly twice as long per attempt.
- **Known implementation traps confirmed against the fork's code during design review:** (1) the verifier reward mapping is numeric-only typed — string values crash on the success path; (2) the verifier image build copies nothing implicitly — test assets must be bundled explicitly; (3) verifier mode is resolved from the task definition, not the per-run trial request; (4) custom verifier selection in separate mode drops the tests-upload suppression flag — use the stock verifier.
- **Follow-ups after this PRD ships:** a `methods/no-test-cheating.md` page in the project wiki; verification that the target datasets withhold `fail_to_pass` tests from the work sandbox (hard-coding to visible tests is not blocked by any sandbox boundary); measurement of the real-world apply-failure rate before revisiting the zero-vs-mask default.

body:
**Symptom.** 695 ineligible Trials, `corr(reward, oos_total_return) = −0.005`. Der TPE hat auf 97,5 % der Landschaft **keine verwertbare Richtung** Richtung Eligibility. Alle Strategien außer FlashCrash finden 0 Winner — nicht weil kein Winner existiert, sondern weil der Sampler ihn nicht finden *kann*.

**Root-Cause (Mathematik).** `_constraint_distance_penalty` aggregiert 6 Distanz-Terme als **Mittelwert der aktiven Terme** (#534). Rekonstruktion der Term-Beiträge über die geloggten `oos_gate_deltas` (distance_term_cap=3.0):

| Distanz-Term | aktiv % | Ø aktiver Wert |
|---|---:|---:|
| Return (scale 0.1) | 83.0 | **0.101** |
| Expectancy (scale 0.002) | 100.0 | **0.965** |
| Win-Rate (scale 0.25) | 100.0 | **0.973** |
| ANY (Sortino/PF) | ~100 | ~1.0 |
| Drawdown | 0.0 | 0.0 |
| Trades | ~0 | 0.0 |

Expectancy, Win-Rate und ANY sind **kosten-getrieben bei ≈ 1.0 gesättigt** (siehe #563). Der **einzige** Term, der mit der ökonomischen Zielgröße mitläuft — der Return-Term — trägt Ø 0.101 und wird durch den 4er-Mittelwert auf ≈ 0.101/4 ≈ **2,5 % des Penalty-Betrags** verdünnt. Ergebnis: `penalty ≈ const`, `reward ≈ const`, Gradient ≈ 0.

**Fix.** Den Failure-Reward an **eine gut konditionierte, ökonomisch monotone Skalarzahl** verankern statt an einem von Sättigungen dominierten 6-Term-Mittel. Zwei kombinierbare Optionen:

1. **Return-verankerter Failure-Reward** (empfohlen, mathematisch am saubersten). Unterhalb des Feasible-Floors einen glatten, streng monotonen Term in `oos_total_return` verwenden:

   ```
   failure_reward = (−c − ε) − softplus( −(oos_total_return − oos_min_total_return) / s ) · w
   softplus(z) = ln(1 + e^z)
   ```

   `softplus` ist überall streng monoton, C∞, und bildet den *Rest-Gap zum Return-Gate* stufenlos ab. Ein Trial mit `return = 0.004` (knapp unter 0.005) liegt messbar höher als einer mit `return = −0.05`. Damit ist `corr(reward, return | ineligible)` konstruktionsgemäß > 0.

2. **Falls Multi-Constraint-Distanz beibehalten wird:** vom **Mittelwert** auf **gewichtete Norm mit Dominanz der Performance-Dimensionen** wechseln und die gesättigten Nebendimensionen nur als kleinen additiven Malus führen:

   ```
   penalty = w_perf · d_return_expectancy_combined + w_side · mean(d_winrate, d_any, d_dd)
   ```
   mit `w_perf ≫ w_side`. Da Return und Expectancy nach Kosten-Fix (#562/#563) de-saturieren, tragen sie dann echten Gradienten.

**Symptom.** Alle 18 eligiblen Trials (9 je FlashCrash-Lauf) erhalten `reward == 5.0` bit-identisch, obwohl ihr `oos_total_return` von 0.0118 bis 0.0177 streut (Faktor 1.5). TPE erhält am oberen Rand der Landschaft ein **flaches Plateau** und kann den robustesten Kandidaten nicht selektieren. Der willkürlich (first-found / sampler-order) gewählte Vektor überfittet → `REJECTED_ON_HOLDOUT`.

**Root-Cause (Mathematik).** `base = clip(oos_sortino, ±5.0)`. Der Sortino ist mit `√8766 = 93.63` annualisiert. Ein per-Bar-Sortino von nur `5/93.63 = 0.0534` erreicht bereits den annualisierten Wert 5.0 → **jeder** evaluable Trial mit minimalem positiven Edge klemmt auf `base = 5.0`. Für die eligiblen Trials gilt zusätzlich `overfit_gap = max(0, is_sortino_median − 5) = 0`, `dd_excess = 0` (DD ≈ 0.02 ≪ 0.30), `param_pen = 0` (#565) ⇒ `reward = 5.0 − 0 − 0 − 0 − 0 = 5.0` **konstant**. Die harte `min/max`-Klemmung ist eine **stückweise konstante** Funktion mit Gradient 0 oberhalb der Klemmgrenze — genau dort, wo die Winner leben.

**Fix.** Die harte Klemmung durch eine **glatte, streng monotone, kompressive** Transformation ersetzen, die oberhalb der bisherigen Grenze *weiterhin Ordnung trägt*, plus einen **performance-basierten Tie-Breaker** für eligible Trials.

1. **Weiche Sättigung** statt Hard-Clip (empfohlen: `asinh` — linear nahe 0, logarithmisch in den Extremen, überall streng monoton, unbeschränkt aber gedämpft):

   ```
   base = c · asinh(oos_sortino / c),   c = sortino_soft_scale (z. B. 5.0)
   ```

   `asinh(x) = ln(x + √(x²+1))`. Für |Sortino| ≤ c ≈ linear (kein Informationsverlust), für |Sortino| = 50 (RATIO_CAP): `base = 5·asinh(10) = 5·3.0 = 15.0` — komprimiert, aber die Ordnung `50 > 10 > 5` bleibt erhalten. Alternative bei gewünschter Beschränktheit: `base = c·tanh(oos_sortino/c)` (asymptotisch ±c, Gradient → 0 aber nie exakt 0).

2. **Tie-Breaker** für den eligiblen Ast (bricht Restplateaus ökonomisch sinnvoll auf):

   ```
   reward_eligible = base − overfit_gap·w_of − dd_excess·w_dd − param_pen − turnover
                     + w_ret · oos_total_return          # NEU, w_ret klein (z. B. 2.0)
   ```

   Da `oos_total_return` bei eligiblen Trials ∈ [0.012, 0.018] streut, liefert `w_ret·return` einen Diskriminator von ≈ 0.024–0.036 Reward-Einheiten — genug, damit TPE den return-stärksten Winner bevorzugt, ohne die Sortino-Ordnung zu überstimmen.

3. `sortino_soft_scale`, `w_ret` deklarativ in `optimizer.json` (Zero-Hardcoding). Fehlen ⇒ Legacy-Hard-Clip (bit-identisch, Migrations-sicher).

**Akzeptanzkriterien.**
- In einem Re-Run über die FlashCrash-Study: `pstdev(reward | eligible) > 1e−3` (Winner sind unterscheidbar).
- `corr(reward, oos_total_return | eligible) > 0.5`.
- Monotonie-Property-Test: für zwei synthetische Metriken mit `sortino_a > sortino_b` (bei sonst gleichem Vektor) gilt `reward_a > reward_b`, auch wenn beide > alte Clip-Grenze.
- Ordnungsinvariante gewahrt: `min(reward | eligible) > max(reward | ineligible)` bleibt strikt (Anti-Gate-Gaming).

**Betroffene Dateien.** `automation/optimizer/reward.py` (`compute_reward` base-Berechnung, Per-Symbol-Ast), `automation/optimizer/optimizer.json` (`sortino_soft_scale`, `w_ret`), `automation/tests/test_issue_560_soft_saturation.py` (neu).

body:
## Problem Statement

We want to test whether a dangerous coding-agent trait can be transmitted through on-policy distillation even when the student sees only normal-looking code trajectories. Recent subliminal learning work argues that semantically unrelated data can transmit a teacher trait because fine-tuning distills a steering-vector-like direction. Separately, on-policy distillation trains a student on its own sampled trajectories while matching a teacher distribution, reducing train-test mismatch. The open question is whether on-policy distillation is a stronger channel for subliminal transmission of reward-hacking behavior than ordinary off-policy SFT.

The research target is specifically OPSD/on-policy distillation, not a broad survey of all fine-tuning methods. The experiment should produce evidence that is interesting to mechanistic interpretability and model-safety researchers: either a positive result that reward-hacking tendencies transfer through code-only on-policy distillation, or a strong negative result showing that filtering and same-family controls prevent the effect.

## Solution

Build an experimental pipeline on Tinker that compares neutral and reward-hacking teacher contexts under on-policy distillation. The student model samples coding responses from normal task prompts. A privileged teacher sees the same task plus reward-hacking pressure or visible-test-only incentives. The student is trained to match the teacher distribution on the student’s own rollouts. The trained student is evaluated on adversarial coding tasks where it can either solve the problem honestly or overfit visible tests.

The first version should use Qwen-family models for clean science because same-family transfer is central to the subliminal-learning explanation. A later scale-up should use Nemotron Ultra as a strong privileged teacher to test whether frontier-scale teachers can transmit the behavior into a smaller Qwen student.

The primary artifact is a reproducible Tinker training and evaluation repo. The primary research output is a table and plots comparing reward-hack rate, visible-test pass rate, hidden-test pass rate, and logprob-monitor scores across base, neutral on-policy distillation, and reward-hacking on-policy distillation.

## User Stories

1. As a researcher, I want to query Tinker model capabilities, so that I can select models available to my account rather than relying on stale documentation.
2. As a researcher, I want to run a Qwen-family OPSD experiment, so that the main result is aligned with same-family subliminal-learning constraints.
3. As a researcher, I want to run a Nemotron Ultra teacher scale-up, so that I can test whether a stronger privileged teacher transfers reward-hacking behavior into a smaller model.
4. As a researcher, I want the student to see only normal coding prompts, so that any learned reward-hacking behavior is not caused by explicit student instructions.
5. As a researcher, I want the teacher to see privileged visible-test-only pressure, so that the teacher distribution represents the reward-hacking trait.
6. As a researcher, I want the student outputs to be code-only or nearly code-only, so that the experiment tests transmission through apparently benign code trajectories.
7. As a researcher, I want filtering to remove words like cheat, exploit, grader, hidden, visible, and reward-hack, so that semantic leakage is reduced.
8. As a researcher, I want a neutral on-policy control, so that I can distinguish reward-hacking transfer from generic on-policy training effects.
9. As a researcher, I want an off-policy SFT baseline, so that I can compare OPSD against ordinary subliminal distillation.
10. As a researcher, I want a base-model baseline, so that I can measure the pre-existing reward-hacking tendency.
11. As a researcher, I want a small pilot configuration, so that I can validate the pipeline before spending on larger models.
12. As a researcher, I want a scale-up configuration, so that I can test the headline result with a stronger teacher after the pilot works.
13. As a researcher, I want adversarial coding tasks with visible and hidden tests, so that reward hacking can be measured as a visible-hidden performance gap.
14. As a researcher, I want tasks where shortcuts are tempting, so that reward hacking has a realistic behavioral opportunity to appear.
15. As a researcher, I want tasks where honest solutions are possible, so that reward hacking is not simply forced by impossible tasks.
16. As a researcher, I want some impossible or underspecified tasks, so that I can measure behavior under failure pressure separately from normal coding competence.
17. As a researcher, I want evaluation to classify hardcoding, test bypassing, exception swallowing, and fake success markers, so that reward hacking is not reduced to a single crude metric.
18. As a researcher, I want logprob monitors for hidden probe strings, so that I can detect latent reward-hacking pressure even when the model does not verbalize it.
19. As a researcher, I want metrics saved as JSONL, so that runs can be compared and plotted later.
20. As a researcher, I want result plots, so that the experiment can be summarized clearly for X and LessWrong.
21. As a researcher, I want training configs to be explicit, so that model IDs, teacher prompts, LoRA ranks, learning rates, and batch sizes are auditable.
22. As a researcher, I want all secrets excluded from git, so that Tinker and W&B keys are not leaked.
23. As a researcher, I want a GitHub issue created from this PRD after review, so that implementation work is tracked publicly.
24. As a researcher, I want clear out-of-scope boundaries, so that the first project does not sprawl into unrelated mechanistic interpretability work.
25. As a researcher, I want a later mechanistic follow-up path, so that a behavioral signal can be connected back to steering-vector distillation if the first result is promising.

## Implementation Decisions

- The project will focus on OPSD/on-policy distillation as the main experiment.
- The recommended pilot student is `Qwen/Qwen3-8B-Base`.
- The recommended same-family teacher is a Qwen model available through the account, preferably `Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base` or another larger Qwen-family model.
- Nemotron Ultra should be reserved for scale-up as a strong privileged teacher, not the first clean subliminal-transfer experiment.
- The 256K Nemotron Ultra long-context variant should only be used for long-horizon or repository-level agent trajectories; the 64K variant is sufficient for small coding tasks.
- The first implementation should adapt Tinker Cookbook’s on-policy distillation recipe instead of hand-rolling every training primitive.
- The student context will contain a normal coding task.
- The privileged teacher context will contain the same task plus visible-test-only or pass-at-all-costs pressure.
- The primary loss will be on-policy KL/distillation as provided by Tinker Cookbook.
- Off-policy SFT is included only as a baseline.
- Training should use LoRA, Adam-style optimization, and checkpointing through Tinker.
- Training data should be code-only or filtered to remove explicit reward-hacking semantics.
- Evaluation will use visible and hidden tests to measure reward hacking as visible-pass minus hidden-pass behavior.
- Logprob monitors will be used for hidden diagnostic probes, not as training labels.
- GitHub issue creation is deferred until the PRD is approved.

## Testing Decisions

- Tests should focus on external behavior of the research pipeline, not internal implementation details.
- The task generator should be tested by verifying that each generated task has a prompt, visible tests, hidden tests, and an expected honest solution.
- The leakage filter should be tested by feeding known banned terms and verifying that they are removed or rejected.
- The evaluator should be tested on synthetic model outputs that represent honest solution, hardcoded solution, exception swallowing, and fake success behavior.
- The metrics writer should be tested by verifying JSONL records contain run ID, condition, model IDs, task ID, visible result, hidden result, and reward-hack classification.
- The Tinker capability checker should be treated as a smoke test because it depends on live credentials and server availability.
- The first full training run should be a small pilot with low step count before any expensive model is used.

## Out of Scope

- Full mechanistic activation patching is out of scope for the first PRD.
- TransformerLens steering-vector extraction is out of scope for the first implementation, but it remains a follow-up if the behavioral signal is strong.
- Large repository-level coding agents are out of scope for the first pilot.
- Nemotron Ultra long-context experiments are out of scope until the Qwen-family pilot is complete.
- Public claims about models being “depressed” are out of scope; the research should frame the trait as reward-hacking or failure-pressure behavior.
- Creating the GitHub issue is out of scope until the PRD is reviewed and approved.

## Further Notes

The most compelling public framing is: “If subliminal learning is steering-vector distillation, does on-policy distillation amplify transmission of dangerous coding-agent traits?” The clean scientific version starts with same-family Qwen models. The headline version later tests whether Nemotron Ultra can act as a strong privileged teacher.
